Pregnancy

Tingling and numbness in pregnancy: hands, back, legs and when to get help

Updated: November 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Pins and needles, burning or reduced feeling can affect the hands, fingers, back, buttocks, thighs or feet during pregnancy. Pressure on a nerve can be one explanation, but location, timing and accompanying symptoms matter. New or persistent symptoms deserve discussion with your maternity team; pregnancy alone does not establish that numbness is harmless. Sudden neurological changes or the emergency signs below need immediate help.

Describe the feeling and its pattern

Tingling may feel like prickling, crawling or burning; numbness means reduced feeling. Brief pins and needles after sitting or sleeping on a body part can settle when pressure is removed. Repeated episodes, a sensation that does not go away, pain or loss of function need an assessment rather than an assumption that every sensation is a normal pregnancy change.

Notice which fingers or part of the leg are affected, whether one or both sides are involved, and whether symptoms occur at night, on waking or during a particular activity. Tell the clinician about weakness, dropping objects, walking difficulty or a change in bladder or bowel control. These details help distinguish possible causes; an online symptom map cannot diagnose them.

Why pregnancy can change nerve symptoms

Pregnancy-related fluid retention can increase pressure around the median nerve in the wrist. Changes in posture, load and the growing abdomen can also affect comfort and put pressure on particular nerves. Ligaments naturally soften during pregnancy and this can contribute to back or pelvic strain, but back pain and nerve-related tingling are not automatically the same problem.

It is too simple to blame every symptom on weight, hormones or relaxin, or to assume that ligament softening proves joint inflammation or nerve damage. Symptoms can have causes unrelated to pregnancy, including a pre-existing nerve problem, vitamin deficiency, another medical condition or a medicine. Assessment should follow the pattern and your history, without blaming you for normal body changes.

Hands and fingers: when carpal tunnel is a possibility

Carpal tunnel syndrome means pressure on the median nerve as it passes through the wrist. Pregnancy swelling can contribute, often later in pregnancy, although symptoms can start earlier. Tingling, numbness or pain may affect one or both hands, particularly the thumb, index and middle fingers, and can be worse at night or first thing in the morning.

A weak grip, difficulty with small tasks or dropping objects also matters. Pain may extend into the arm, but not every hand, shoulder or neck symptom comes from the wrist. Tell the clinician about earlier carpal tunnel, an injury or another condition such as diabetes or thyroid disease. Your symptoms need their own assessment, regardless of how common carpal tunnel is in pregnancy.

Protect the wrist while arranging advice

A correctly fitted wrist splint can keep the wrist neutral during sleep. Avoid holding it tightly bent forwards or backwards; reduce or pace repeated gripping and other activities that aggravate symptoms, with regular breaks. Resting the forearm on a pillow and gentle hand movement may help. Remove rings early if swelling develops, rather than waiting until they become tight.

Ask a physiotherapist or pharmacist about fit and skin checks; loosen or remove a splint that causes pressure, discomfort or worsening numbness and seek advice. If cold is suggested, use a wrapped pack and follow professional instructions. Reduced sensation makes it harder to judge temperature: do not apply heat or ice to an area you cannot feel normally without advice. Be careful carrying hot drinks when grip or feeling is impaired.

Back, buttock and leg symptoms need their own assessment

Sciatica describes irritation or compression of the sciatic nerve, often causing pain, tingling, numbness or weakness from the buttock down the back of one leg, sometimes into the foot. Backache alone is not usually sciatica. Ordinary pregnancy back or pelvic strain can coexist with it, but there is no basis here for calling sciatica the cause of most pregnancy tingling.

Discuss persistent or worsening symptoms and difficulty with daily activities with your maternity team or clinician. Back pain in the second or third trimester, or with fever, vaginal bleeding, urinary pain or pain in the side under the ribs, needs urgent advice. New loss of feeling with back pain has a separate emergency pathway below; do not wait for a routine physiotherapy appointment.

An outer-thigh patch can have a different cause

Meralgia paraesthetica involves the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, a sensory nerve near the groin. It can cause a patch of tingling, numbness, burning or sensitivity to light touch on the outer thigh, usually on one side. Pregnancy-related pressure or tight clothing can contribute; standing, walking or lying on that side may worsen it.

This nerve supplies sensation, not muscle movement. Leg weakness, loss of walking ability or a different distribution should not be explained away as meralgia. A clinician can assess the pattern. Loose clothing, avoiding a tight belt, pacing prolonged standing and using a pillow or the more comfortable side may help. Symptoms often ease after birth, but persistence still deserves review.

Comfort measures should fit the cause and your pregnancy

Change uncomfortable positions, support your back and limbs, and avoid long uninterrupted periods in one position. Gentle movement and activity within your maternity advice may help; prolonged bed rest is not a general treatment for nerve symptoms. A pregnancy-experienced physiotherapist can choose appropriate exercises and adaptations rather than applying one stretch to every numb area.

Gentle massage or a comfortably warm bath may ease muscular back discomfort, but does not prove that a compressed nerve has been treated. Avoid deep massage of a painful or swollen leg while a clot is possible, and do not use hot or cold packs on skin with reduced feeling without advice. Stop an activity that worsens symptoms and seek the appropriate assessment instead of pushing through new weakness or loss of sensation.

What an assessment and treatment plan may involve

The clinician may check sensation, strength, reflexes, movement, the wrist and back, alongside your pregnancy and medical history. Blood tests may be appropriate when a vitamin, iron, glucose or other problem is suspected. Carpal tunnel is often assessed from symptoms and examination; nerve-conduction tests or imaging are considered when the diagnosis is uncertain, not required for every pregnant person.

Treatment depends on the cause. Splints, activity changes and physiotherapy may be enough for some people; persistent or worsening carpal tunnel can lead to discussion of an injection or specialist care. Check every pain medicine with a pregnancy-aware professional. Paracetamol may be suitable when advised, but does not remove nerve compression. Do not independently start oral or injected NSAIDs such as ibuprofen: risks change with gestation, including avoidance from 20 weeks unless clinically necessary and third-trimester contraindication in UK guidance.

Iron deficiency and restless legs are not the same as numbness

Restless legs syndrome usually brings an urge to move with uncomfortable sensations, often worse during rest in the evening or at night. Moving may temporarily help. Pregnancy and low iron can be associated with it. A fixed patch of lost feeling or muscle weakness is a different finding and should not simply be labelled restless legs.

If symptoms disrupt sleep or everyday wellbeing, discuss them with your clinician. They may consider iron levels, medicines and other possible causes. Iron treatment is useful when indicated, not a universal cure for tingling. Do not increase supplements or start a medicine for restless legs from a general adult treatment list; pregnancy needs its own review.

Vitamin B12 deserves separate attention

Vitamin B12 deficiency can affect nerves, causing pins and needles, numbness, muscle weakness or balance and coordination problems. These neurological symptoms can occur without established anaemia. They are not interchangeable with the association between iron deficiency and restless legs.

Tell the clinician about diet, relevant conditions, medicines and any previous deficiency, but do not diagnose yourself from a symptom list. Examination and appropriate blood tests help guide treatment. Seek assessment promptly for suspected neurological symptoms: untreated B12 deficiency can cause lasting harm. A routine supplement does not replace finding and treating the cause.

Does tingling mean gestational diabetes is uncontrolled?

No. Gestational diabetes usually has no symptoms and is identified through the recommended glucose-testing pathway. Tingling alone neither diagnoses it nor shows how well it is controlled. Diabetic nerve damage is more associated with longer-standing diabetes; that is not a reason to assume that new pregnancy tingling is diabetic neuropathy.

Keep your planned antenatal tests and, if you already have diabetes, follow the agreed glucose-monitoring and treatment plan. Report new symptoms and review actual results with the team rather than changing medicine or food intake on the basis of tingling. Persistent thirst, unusually frequent urination or other concerns also deserve advice, but symptoms cannot replace testing.

Could swelling or tingling signal pre-eclampsia?

Tingling on its own does not diagnose pre-eclampsia or rule it out. Blood pressure and urine checks at antenatal visits can identify signs you may not feel. A swollen wrist may have a local nerve explanation, but that should not cancel assessment of a new maternity warning symptom.

Get immediate maternity advice for a severe headache, especially one not relieved by simple painkillers; visual problems; pain below the ribs; sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet; feeling very unwell; heartburn that does not improve with medicine; or vomiting. Do not wait for these signs to occur together or for tingling to accompany them. Tell the team about other changes such as reduced urine as well. A first seizure or loss of consciousness is an emergency.

Pregnancy symptoms that should not wait

Contact your maternity team immediately for any vaginal bleeding, leaking fluid, reduced or changed usual fetal movements, or possible premature labour. Before 37 weeks, regular contractions or tightenings, period-like pains or unusual backache need contact even if they are not painful. Abdominal pain with bleeding, lower-back pain, unusual discharge or fluid leakage, urinary symptoms, or severe or persistent pain also needs immediate advice.

Call emergency services for heavy vaginal bleeding, or bleeding with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness. These are alternative warning signs; bleeding need not be heavy when one of the associated signs is present. Do not drive yourself to emergency care: ask someone to take you or call an ambulance. Do not wait for a sensory symptom to settle before seeking help.

Neurological and clot warning signs need urgent action

Call emergency services for sudden stroke-like symptoms, such as weakness or numbness on one side, a drooping face, speech or visual disturbance, confusion or sudden loss of balance, even if they stop. Seek emergency assessment for back pain with loss of feeling in one or both legs, the bottom or genitals; sciatica on both sides; severe or worsening weakness or numbness in both legs; or new difficulty starting or controlling urine, inability to urinate, or loss of bowel awareness or control. A first seizure also needs an ambulance; do not wait five minutes for a first seizure.

New leg pain or swelling, particularly on one side or with colour changes, needs urgent assessment for a possible clot rather than massage or a wait-and-see exercise trial. Sudden breathing difficulty, chest or upper-back pain, a very fast heartbeat, or fainting/loss of consciousness needs emergency help, with or without leg symptoms. Coughing up blood needs urgent advice. Do not drive yourself in an emergency; arrange another driver or ambulance. Follow an existing seizure plan where applicable, but obtain emergency help for a seizure longer than usual; a seizure lasting more than five minutes if its usual duration is unknown; failure to regain full consciousness or repeated seizures without recovery; serious injury; or breathing difficulty.

Keep a follow-up plan rather than a reassurance deadline

Ask what diagnosis is most likely, which measures to try, what changes should trigger another call and when to review if symptoms persist. Explain how sleep, work, walking, grip and baby-care tasks are affected. Supportive treatment should make life more manageable while the team checks for causes that need specific care.

Pregnancy-related carpal tunnel and meralgia often improve after birth, but recovery varies and symptoms may last longer. Do not accept a guarantee that delivery will instantly cure every nerve symptom. Ask for reassessment of persistent numbness, weakness or functional difficulty after birth, and for help adapting feeding and lifting positions safely.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Describe the exact area, timing, triggers and effect on grip or walking to your maternity team; ask which diagnosis and examination or tests fit the pattern.

Have wrist supports and exercises checked for your pregnancy. Confirm safe skin care and medicine choices instead of copying a general adult pain plan.

Agree a review date and urgent contact route, continue antenatal screening and act on warning signs without waiting for all symptoms or a planned appointment.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record where symptoms occur, their timing, medicines, test appointments and questions for your care team. It cannot diagnose a trapped nerve, interpret neurological signs or glucose and blood-pressure results, choose medicines or decide that a symptom is a normal pregnancy change. Recording must not delay maternity or emergency care.

When to seek help

Seek immediate maternity advice for bleeding, leaking fluid, changed movements, possible premature labour or pre-eclampsia warning signs. Heavy bleeding alone, or bleeding with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness, needs emergency help. Sudden stroke-like symptoms, a first seizure, back pain with loss of leg/bottom/genital feeling, bilateral sciatica, severe/worsening bilateral deficits or new bladder/bowel dysfunction also need emergency assessment. Sudden breathing difficulty, chest/upper-back pain, very fast heartbeat or passing out is an emergency even without leg symptoms. New leg pain or swelling needs urgent clot assessment. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; arrange another driver or an ambulance. Do not use home remedies to delay assessment.

Evidence notes updated: November 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Location, timing, strength and accompanying symptoms matter more than a single label for pregnancy tingling.
  • Carpal tunnel, sciatica and outer-thigh sensory nerve pressure have different patterns and care plans.
  • Neutral wrist support, pacing and pregnancy-appropriate physiotherapy may help; protect skin with reduced sensation.
  • Iron-related restless legs, B12 deficiency and diabetes questions require their own assessment, not symptom-based self-diagnosis.
  • Act immediately on maternity or neurological warning signs; do not delay emergency care while trying home remedies.

Frequently asked questions

Can gestational diabetes cause tingling in my hands or feet?

Diabetes can be associated with nerve problems, particularly when longstanding, but tingling alone does not diagnose gestational diabetes or prove poor control. Gestational diabetes is usually found by glucose testing. Keep your antenatal screening and agreed glucose-monitoring plan, and report new symptoms for assessment.

Could tingling be a sign of pre-eclampsia?

Tingling alone cannot diagnose or exclude it. Keep blood-pressure and urine checks. Seek immediate maternity advice for severe headache, visual problems, pain below the ribs, sudden face/hand/foot swelling, feeling very unwell, heartburn unrelieved by medicine or vomiting; do not wait for all signs. A first seizure or loss of consciousness needs emergency help.

Can anaemia explain pins and needles?

Low iron may be associated with restless legs, which usually involves an urge to move during rest. B12 deficiency can cause true neurological symptoms, sometimes without anaemia. These are different problems. Ask about appropriate assessment and tests rather than treating every numb sensation with extra iron or vitamins.

When should I contact a doctor or midwife?

Report new, persistent, recurrent or worsening symptoms, especially weakness or difficulty using a limb. Maternity warning symptoms need immediate contact. Sudden stroke-like changes, a first seizure, loss of consciousness, back pain with loss of leg/bottom/genital feeling or new bladder/bowel changes need emergency care. Sudden breathlessness or chest/upper-back pain also needs emergency help; do not drive yourself.

Can I use a wrist splint for night-time hand tingling?

It may help suspected carpal tunnel by holding the wrist neutral. Ask about fit and skin checks and reduce aggravating activities. A splint does not diagnose the cause; seek review if symptoms worsen, grip weakens or measures do not help.

Is a numb patch on the outside of my thigh sciatica?

Not necessarily. A sensory nerve near the groin can cause meralgia paraesthetica in that area. Sciatica more often runs through the buttock down the back of the leg. Neither label should explain away new weakness, walking difficulty or emergency warning signs.

Are massage, heat or painkillers always safe?

No. Comfort depends on the cause, skin sensation and pregnancy. Do not massage a possibly clotted painful/swollen leg or apply heat/ice where feeling is reduced without advice. Check medicines with a pregnancy-aware professional; general ibuprofen advice for nonpregnant adults does not apply automatically.

Will symptoms disappear as soon as my baby is born?

Some pregnancy-related nerve-pressure symptoms improve as swelling and pressure reduce, but the timing varies. Persistent numbness, weakness or difficulty with daily tasks deserves reassessment and a follow-up plan rather than an instant-cure promise.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
